It was then that Trump asked her to run for a full six-year term, something she said she hadn’t previously considered. Now polls show her tied with or trailing Democrat Annie Andrews, making South Carolina competitive in a way it hasn’t been for decades. “It’s just been absolutely brutal,” Graham said, referencing how she lost her brother and competed in three elections in a span of months. Josh Dawsey spent the day with Graham on the campaign trail as she fights to keep her brother’s seat .

   • Ahead of Election Day, follow our live coverage for the latest developments and analysis.

Muse could disrupt Amazon’s model by finding and buying products, effectively bypassing the human browsing experience. The threat lies in Muse’s potential to undermine one of Amazon’s most lucrative businesses: advertising . Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site shortly after its launch, citing safety concerns, report Isabella Simonetti and Suzanne Vranica.

The Journal’s Hannah Miao visited the place they call “Dalifornia” to try to understand the disillusionment among young people in the country. Investors Are Hedging Against the Risks of the AI Boom
 
Plus, inside the final days of Darline Graham’s reluctant Senate run, and two owners claim to have the same legendary Porsche
 
 
JASON HENRY FOR WSJ
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Some tech employees have made so much money from the AI boom that they’re quitting their jobs. Not to retire or pursue a passion project, but to hedge their company stock.

 

It’s a striking sign of how nervous some investors have become about Wall Street’s multitrillion-dollar bet on artificial intelligence. The trade has been enormously profitable, but recent disappointments have prompted investors and tech executives to seek protection against a larger unraveling. They’re turning to options and credit-default swaps, while trading firms are developing new derivatives tied to the price of computing power.

 

As one trader puts it: “I don’t think my house is going to catch on fire, but I still have insurance.” Gunjan Banerji reports on the growing demand for protection against the AI trade’s risks.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• A lot of voters are heading to the polls Tuesday hoping for a fix for affordability. They are going to be disappointed, writes our chief economics commentator Greg Ip.

 

• When Irfan Al-Hussaini, a data scientist at Nvidia, died at age 32 in July, the medical examiner ruled his death a suicide. His family has challenged the ruling and is calling for an investigation.

 

• Our reporters asked one couple to show us how they master open enrollment by comparing their respective employer plans to find the most cost-effective coverage for their family.

 

• Binance began allowing customers to resume withdrawals from its exchange after racing to cover its losses in the biggest cyber heist in history.

 

• Anthropic will soon join other hot tech companies in going public with a share structure that keeps founders in control. It’s the Age of the Imperial CEO, writes business columnist Tim Higgins.

 

• Los Angeles, run by Democratic mayors for a quarter-century, is in a rut. Voters are mulling whether a Democratic socialist might be able to dig it out.

 
 
 

3. FROM THE MARKETS

 

• The circular financing underpinning AI took a step into the big league last week with the decision by chip makers Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom to act as $5 billion cornerstone investors in Meta Platforms’ $25 billion stock sale. This circularity is part of a worrying growth in interconnections between AI companies, writes columnist James Mackintosh.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Inside the final days of Darline Graham’s reluctant Senate run.

 

Darline Graham had just been sworn in to finish her late brother’s Senate term when she was in the Oval Office trying to coax President Trump to support Lindsey Graham’s Russia sanctions bill. It was then that Trump asked her to run for a full six-year term, something she said she hadn’t previously considered. Now polls show her tied with or trailing Democrat Annie Andrews, making South Carolina competitive in a way it hasn’t been for decades. “It’s just been absolutely brutal,” Graham said, referencing how she lost her brother and competed in three elections in a span of months. Josh Dawsey spent the day with Graham on the campaign trail as she fights to keep her brother’s seat.

 

• Ahead of Election Day, follow our live coverage for the latest developments and analysis.

 

5.

 

AI shopping bots are coming for Amazon’s business.

 

Amazon has long been the first stop for many online shoppers, but Meta just built a new one in the form of its personal AI agent, Muse. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada set up the agents in Muse’s first month and a half, the company said. Muse could disrupt Amazon’s model by finding and buying products, effectively bypassing the human browsing experience. The threat lies in Muse’s potential to undermine one of Amazon’s most lucrative businesses: advertising. Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site shortly after its launch, citing safety concerns, report Isabella Simonetti and Suzanne Vranica.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Two owners claim to have the same legendary Porsche.

 
 
RAINER SCHLEGELMILCH/GETTY IMAGES
 

One of the world’s most famous Porsches is a race car painted in a psychedelic swirl of purples and greens. Known as the “Hippie Car,” it stunned the racing world in 1970 by beating Ferrari at Le Mans. What it is potentially worth is unclear, but these days, masterpieces of motor sports history are selling for Pablo Picasso prices. Now, two owners think they have it. One purple-and-green Porsche is housed in a Philadelphia museum; the other belongs to a former race car driver. With tens of millions of dollars potentially at stake, which one is the real deal?

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING THIS WEEK

 

• Monday: The ISM releases its October manufacturing index. Apple and Palantir Technologies report earnings.

 

• Tuesday: Americans head to the polls for the midterm elections, with control of Congress at stake. The Labor Department releases September job openings. AMD, Shopify, Pfizer report earnings.

 

• Wednesday: ADP releases its October private-sector employment report, and the ISM releases its services index. Uber, Qualcomm, CVS Health, Novo Nordisk and McDonald’s report earnings.

 

• Thursday: The Bank of England announces its latest interest-rate decision. Airbnb reports earnings.

 

• Friday: The Labor Department releases the October jobs report. Pope Leo XIV begins a 12-day visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Moderna reports earnings.

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
$12 billion
 

Candidates and their backers are spending nearly this much in the midterm cycle, making it the most expensive in history, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact. Then there are candidates who have somehow managed to stay dry amid a deluge of dollars. Some of them are dodging rodents and pawning power tools just to stay afloat.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Our reporter traveled to China’s laid-back capital of doing nothing.

 

In recent years, the charming town of Dali in southern China’s Yunnan province became known as the place where young Chinese people go to escape the rat race and “lie flat”—giving up on work or generally doing the bare minimum. The Journal’s Hannah Miao visited the place they call “Dalifornia” to try to understand the disillusionment among young people in the country. What she found was that many of these drifters were tired of doing nothing. They wanted to get back to work.
